isotopes.story: Living things constantly exchange carbon with the atmosphere, keeping the ratio of C-14 to C-12 roughly constant. When something dies, C-14 starts decaying. Measuring the remaining ratio tells you how long ago death occurred — this is radiocarbon dating, which has revolutionized archaeology.

U-238's half-life is roughly the age of the Earth. Half of all the U-238 that existed when Earth formed is still here. The other half has decayed — through a chain of 14 steps — to lead-206. By measuring the U-238 to Pb-206 ratio in ancient zircon crystals, geologists can date rocks to within millions of years.

U-235 is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope — it can sustain a chain reaction. Natural uranium is only 0.72% U-235; nuclear reactors use enriched uranium (3-5% U-235); weapons use highly enriched uranium (>90%). The 704-million-year half-life means U-235 was far more abundant when Earth formed.

K-40 decays to both calcium-40 and argon-40. The argon-40 that accumulates in rocks and minerals is used for potassium-argon dating — essential for dating volcanic rocks and establishing the geological timescale. The K-40 in your body also contributes to your natural radiation dose.

I-131 concentrates in the thyroid because the thyroid uses iodine to make hormones. Doctors use it to image thyroid function or destroy overactive thyroid tissue. Its short half-life means it disappears from the body in weeks. It's also a major concern in nuclear accidents: Chernobyl and Fukushima both released I-131.

Technetium-99m is the most widely used medical radioisotope in the world. The 'm' stands for 'metastable' — it releases gamma rays without changing element. Its 6-hour half-life is near-perfect: long enough for imaging, short enough that it's mostly gone from the body within a day.

Tritium (H-3) decays to helium-3 with a 12-year half-life. It's used in nuclear weapons as a 'booster' gas, and in self-luminous watch dials and emergency exit signs (tritium glows without batteries). The helium-3 it produces is extremely rare and valuable for scientific instruments.

Polonium-210 generates 140 watts per gram from alpha decay — making it valuable as a compact heat source. It was used to assassinate Alexander Litvinenko in 2006 (the first known case of nuclear terrorism on European soil). A gram of Po-210 would kill about 50 million people if dispersed.

Strontium-90 was one of the most feared components of nuclear fallout during the Cold War. Because it mimics calcium, it deposits in bones, irradiating bone marrow and causing leukemia. Measuring Sr-90 in baby teeth was used as a public health indicator of fallout exposure in the 1950s-60s.
